stories.headline: Oil supertanker ‘sinks after hitting mine’ in Strait of Hormuz
stories.claim: Iran's IRGC says a supertanker sank after hitting a mine in the Strait of Hormuz, with no independent confirmation yet.
stories.summary: Iran's Revolutionary Guards said a supertanker carrying more than two million barrels of crude sank after striking a mine in the Strait of Hormuz, and that a second tanker also hit a mine. The claims, made on state television on Sunday, have not been independently confirmed, and the UK Maritime Trade Operations centre said damage and environmental impact were unknown but the crew were safe. The strait, which normally carries about a fifth of global oil, has been heavily restricted by Iran since the war began in late February, and the US has imposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports and escorted tankers. The same day Iran said it had fired drones at a US radar base in Bahrain, which Bahrain's military said it intercepted. With Donald Trump reportedly planning to raise the conflict at a trilateral meeting with China and Russia this week, the escalation adds pressure on oil prices and shipping insurance.
key_points: The IRGC said a supertanker carrying over two million barrels of crude sank in the southern Persian Gulf after hitting a mine, and a second tanker was also hit.
The UK Maritime Trade Operations centre said the damage and environmental impact were unknown but the crew were safe.
Iran has heavily restricted traffic through the strait since the war began on 28 February, and has often targeted ships not using its authorised routes.
The US Central Command said it had cleared mines from main routes and had been helping Gulf countries export oil through the strait.
On the same day Iran claimed drone attacks on a US base in Bahrain; Bahrain said it intercepted several attacks and no casualties were reported.
stories.market_take: Any real disruption to Hormuz tanker traffic would likely push oil prices higher and lift tanker and insurance stocks.

stories.headline: Body of elderly windsurfer missing off Tanjung Bungah found in Penang marina
stories.claim: Body of missing 74-year-old windsurfing doctor found on rocks off Penang's Tanjung Bungah after two-day search.
stories.summary: The body of Khaw Chun Sein, a 74-year-old doctor, was found on rocks near the Straits Quay Retail Marina in Penang, Malaysia, on 16 November. He had gone missing while windsurfing off Tanjung Bungah the previous evening, after an emergency call was received at 7.42pm on 15 November. A multi-agency search covered 94.76 square nautical miles, using an MMEA helicopter, seven rescue boats and fire and volunteer teams. The body was discovered at 9.56am on the second day of the operation and pronounced dead at the scene, and the search was called off at 10.30am. The case is a local tragedy with no wider significance.

Three potential buyers are in talks, with Martin Property Group the preferred bidder, though progress has stalled over loan repayment terms. Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds plans to meet the parties, and MPs have criticised Gordon Brothers, which denies freezing funds.

stories.headline: Estonia has a plan for Russian occupation: Run its government from the cloud
stories.claim: Estonia is drafting a plan to run its government digitally from abroad, via cloud and data embassies, if its territory is occupied.
stories.summary: Estonia is preparing a national doomsday resilience strategy, called hukukindlus, that would let the government run its digital services from abroad if its territory were occupied by a hostile power. The plan builds on a data backup held in a "digital embassy" in Luxembourg and on cloud systems from Microsoft Azure, Amazon Web Services and the state's own platform. The 1.3 million-strong Baltic state, which shares a 294km border with Russia, has been shaped by its experience of the 2007 cyberattacks that it attributes to Moscow. Officials say the aim is to ensure services and state data survive, and remain usable for decades. The approach reflects a wider European shift towards spreading digital risk across borders, including a new UK-Norway data embassy arrangement.

stories.headline: Rescuers recover last 2 bodies after methane blast kills 4 at a Colombia coal mine
stories.claim: Rescuers recovered the last two bodies after a methane blast at a coal mine in central Colombia killed four people.
stories.summary: Four miners died in a methane explosion at the La Victoria coal mine in Chita, Boyacá, about 240 kilometres north of Bogotá, Colombia. Rescuers recovered two bodies on Saturday and the final two on Sunday, after which search and rescue operations ended. The National Mining Agency says an investigation is continuing and has ordered operations at the site halted. The mine's operator has not been named, though officials say it was properly registered. Colombia's agency has warned repeatedly that gas and dust can build up in coal deposits, and small-scale mines in the region have a long record of accidents. Separately, a worker was killed by a rockfall at another mine in Boyacá.

stories.headline: Minister backs legal right to job support for young people
stories.claim: Milburn review to recommend guaranteed jobs or training for under-25s, while ministers back legal underpinning and tighter benefit rules.
stories.summary: Work and pensions secretary Pat McFadden has backed giving young people a legal guarantee of help getting into work, saying current support is too vague. Former Labour minister Alan Milburn's review, due to be published on Tuesday, will recommend that under-25s be guaranteed a job placement or training. It is also expected to propose ending the health element of universal credit for under-25s, with some eligible for a new additional cost allowance. McFadden confirmed some existing claimants would receive less when reassessed, a move that could split Labour MPs, who blocked a previous benefit cut last year. The Conservatives' Helen Whately rejected the legal guarantee and argued that cutting employer taxes would do more. Separately, the government is widening its subsidised job scheme so that jobless under-25s are offered a role after 12 months rather than 18 from next April.

stories.headline: Bangladesh garment factories shut as workers strike over minimum wage
stories.claim: Garment factories in Bangladesh's Savar, Ashulia and Gazipur hubs have shut as workers strike for a 30,000-taka minimum wage.
stories.summary: Owners in Bangladesh's main garment hubs are moving toward indefinite closures as workers strike over the minimum wage. Nearly 150 factories in Savar, Ashulia and Gazipur shut over the weekend, and employer groups say plants that cannot operate will stay closed indefinitely from Monday under labour law. Earlier reports put the number of affected plants far higher, with owners in Ashulia, Jamgora and Hemayetpur weighing the closure of 210 factories ahead of an emergency meeting, and nine factories in Ashulia and Savar having already shut, affecting about 200,000 workers. Workers are demanding a minimum wage of 30,000 to 32,000 taka a month, up from 12,500 taka, while employers say even 30,000 taka is unaffordable amid high inflation, an energy crisis and new US tariffs. Protests have brought clashes, tear gas, dozens of arrests and more than 500 temporary closures, and a worker reportedly died after being beaten. The sector earns nearly $40bn a year and employs about four million people, supplying H&M, Primark and Zara. A government wage board is due to finish recommendations by the end of November, with any new pay due from 1 December.

stories.headline: India's wholesale inflation accelerates to 12.29% in October on fuel price surge
stories.claim: India's wholesale inflation rose to 12.29% in October, driven by a surge in fuel and power prices.
stories.summary: India's wholesale price inflation accelerated to 12.29% year-on-year in October, up from 11.39% in September and above the 12.1% Reuters poll forecast. The jump was driven by fuel and power, which rose 32.84% after 25.85% in September, while crude petroleum and natural gas prices surged 70.8%. Retail inflation also climbed to 6.09%, breaching the Reserve Bank of India's 6% tolerance limit for the first time in two years, which has raised bets on a rate hike. Economists expect some cooling in November as global energy prices dipped and oil eased toward $95 a barrel. Wholesale food prices rose 8.58%. The data points to continued pressure on the central bank from energy costs.

stories.headline: How the world’s fires changed while humanity hit pause

The drop was steepest in forests, at about 27.7 percent, and smaller in grasslands at 8.4 percent. Some regions saw increases, including 31.4 percent in Colombia, 25.4 percent in India and 70.7 percent in Honduras. The work uses satellite data and treats the pandemic as a natural experiment.

Senate Banking Chairman Tim Scott has written to Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick seeking testimony, and the Remote Access Security Act is being revived, though it may not become law.

stories.headline: Judge blocks Trump administration from closing DC East Potomac golf course for now
stories.claim: A federal judge temporarily blocked the Trump administration from closing East Potomac Park's golf course in Washington for a planned 15-month redevelopment.

In a 30-page decision issued Saturday, Reyes called the government's justifications pretextual and found it had broken at least two federal laws to meet an arbitrary deadline. The order runs through 28 November and requires the park to stay open to the public, although the administration does not have to run golf operations there. Trump said his administration will immediately appeal on an expedited basis, calling the decision highly destructive and political, while the Justice Department said the ruling does not stop planning for the course. The case was brought by the DC Preservation League and others, including two local golfers who argue the redevelopment would make the course unaffordable and change its character. Earlier, the National Park Service cut hundreds of trees in October with only 15 hours' notice to the court, and Reyes has opened an inquiry, with a special master, into whether Justice Department lawyers misled the court. The ruling is one of several court setbacks for Trump's Washington projects, which also include a memorial arch, a White House ballroom and the Kennedy Center.

stories.headline: US manufacturing is back and better

stories.summary: A new Kearney report casts doubt on the White House claim that Trump's tariffs have delivered the largest reshoring wave in American history. stories.claim: Treasury Secretary Bessent called for a 'dramatic shakeup' at Nvidia, an outside CEO, and answers on China-linked chip sales.
stories.summary: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has called for a "dramatic shakeup" at Nvidia and said the chipmaker should hire its next chief executive from outside the company. He demanded that the board and outside counsel answer within 10 days whether Nvidia knowingly ignored warning signs that shell companies, many based in Singapore, were routing advanced AI chips to China. Bessent made the remarks on Fox News and in a CNBC interview, where he questioned whether Nvidia knew its customers were pass-through shell companies and said anyone responsible should be held accountable. He stopped short of saying Jensen Huang knew of the practices, criticised general counsel Timothy Teter for contacting Commerce about the detention of Megaspeed's Alice Wong in Singapore, and said existing export rules should be enforced rather than tightened. He also said Treasury, War, State and USTR backed adding Megaspeed to the Entity List, but that Commerce's BIS reportedly stalled the move over China trade concerns. The intervention is unusual for a cabinet-level official targeting a single company and raises pressure on Nvidia ahead of its results on 17 November.

Designed by the local practice ARCHSTUDIO, led by Han Wenqiang, it transforms a derelict agricultural machinery factory into a public museum. The project sits within the Shu Brocade Heritage Cultural & Creative Park in Banqiao Village, a initiative of the Sichuan Provincial Department of Culture and Tourism. The architects kept the original brick walls, added new roofing, and wove brocade references into the interior through a timber and steel roof, undulating facades and perforated bricks. Inside are temporary and permanent displays and a digital archive of Shu brocade techniques, with gardens planted with traditional dye plants. The scheme is presented as a model for industrial heritage reuse and rural renewal.

stories.claim: Alan Milburn's youth unemployment review will urge phased cuts to employer National Insurance for 21-24-year-olds and tighter benefit rules for under-25s.
stories.summary: A major independent review led by former Labour minister Alan Milburn will recommend gradually cutting employer National Insurance for workers aged 21 to 24, starting with retail and hospitality, to tackle youth unemployment. The report, due for publication on Tuesday, comes after a year of work and is framed around the roughly one million young people in the UK who are not in education, employment or training (Neets). Milburn argues the government spends £22bn a year supporting economically inactive young people and proposes stricter benefit rules, including ending the health element of Universal Credit and Pip for under-25s. The proposals would also test Chancellor John Healey's fiscal room and the Labour government's welfare agenda.
key_points: The review will propose cutting employer NI for 21-24-year-olds over five years, starting with retail and hospitality, which employ 37% of 16-24-year-olds.
Milburn wants the existing NI threshold for 21-24-year-olds doubled from £5,000 to £10,000, but only when fiscal conditions allow.
An immediate scrapping of NI for that age group would cost £5.1bn, according to the Resolution Foundation.
Under-25s would lose eligibility for the health element of Universal Credit and Pip, and a legal job guarantee would tie benefits to taking up help.
Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden said the subsidised jobs guarantee would be extended to 18-24-year-olds on Universal Credit after 12 months, helping over 90,000 people by March 2029.
The Conservatives, through Helen Whately, want employer NI halved, while Milburn backed slowing the convergence of youth minimum wage rates.

stories.headline: Vulcan rocket fails on first Amazon Leo launch, losing 40 satellites and likely grounding rocket
stories.claim: ULA's Vulcan rocket failed on Sunday, losing 40 Amazon Leo satellites, and is expected to be grounded indefinitely.
stories.summary: United Launch Alliance's Vulcan rocket failed about ten minutes into its Sunday launch from Cape Canaveral, losing 40 Amazon Leo broadband satellites. It was the first total mission failure for ULA since it was formed in 2006. The rocket was a custom six-booster Vulcan with a Centaur V upper stage built for low Earth orbit, and the boosters and fairing separated normally before the anomaly. Sources told Ars Technica the fault lay in the booster stage, which kept burning for at least 30 seconds past its planned shutdown, and the Centaur upper stage then tried to correct the spin. ULA says it will investigate the cause and provide updates, and the rocket is expected to be grounded for an indefinite period. The setback hits Amazon's plans to challenge SpaceX's Starlink with its Leo network, which has 396 satellites in orbit against a planned 3,292. Amazon has 37 more Vulcan launches booked, and the grounding threatens US Space Force launches and NASA's Artemis programme. The next mission, LV-02, was due within weeks and is probably on hold.

The Wednesday meeting with Modi was a late addition to the schedule, and the couple last met him during their 2016 visit to India. William said India has produced more Earthshot finalists and winners than any other nation over the past six years.

stories.headline: Mexican drug lord Miguel Angel Felix Gallardo dies age 80
stories.claim: Mexican drug lord Miguel Angel Felix Gallardo, founder of the Guadalajara Cartel, has died in hospital aged 80.
stories.summary: Miguel Angel Felix Gallardo, one of the most notorious drug traffickers in history, has died in hospital in Guadalajara aged 80. Known as the "Boss of Bosses", he led the Guadalajara Cartel, which dominated Mexican drug smuggling during the 1980s cocaine boom. He forged the alliance with Colombian cartels, including Pablo Escobar's Medellin Cartel, that moved cocaine into the United States. He was captured in 1989 and had been in state custody since, and was granted house arrest in 2022 but was never transferred because of ankle-monitor problems. His organisation later split, giving rise to the Sinaloa Cartel led by Joaquin "El Chapo" Guzman. His death closes a chapter in the history of the drug trade.

stories.headline: Trump, Xi and Putin to hold first trilateral meeting at APEC in Shenzhen
stories.claim: China says the planned Trump-Xi-Putin trilateral at APEC in Shenzhen on Thursday is of 'groundbreaking significance'; no agreement is expected.
stories.summary: China's Foreign Ministry said the planned trilateral meeting between Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin, set for Thursday in Shenzhen on the sidelines of the APEC summit, is of 'groundbreaking significance'. It would be the first in-person meeting of the three heads of state. The White House has said nuclear arms reduction will be the main topic, with Iran possibly discussed but Ukraine not expected to be, and a senior US official said no agreement is expected. Trump arrives late on Wednesday for the two-day summit and will hold a bilateral lunch with Xi before the trilateral, their fourth meeting since 2025. The meeting comes after the New START treaty expired in February, leaving no major arms control limits, and China has long resisted nuclear talks involving itself. Beijing has not disclosed the agenda, and UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said the UN would support any denuclearisation effort arising from the talks. Trump is on a four-day Asia trip that also includes a Quad meeting and a US-ASEAN summit in Manila, while commentators have said the Yalta comparison is overblown.

stories.headline: Ousted Bangladesh PM Hasina says she will return home in December despite death sentence
stories.claim: Sheikh Hasina says she will return to Bangladesh in December despite a death sentence handed down in absentia.
stories.summary: Sheikh Hasina, Bangladesh's ousted former prime minister, has told AFP she will return home in December, saying 'no threat of death' will keep her away. Speaking by email from India, where she has been in hiding since fleeing in August 2024, the 79-year-old said she had made up her mind and was already preparing the trip, and her lawyers have applied for a Bangladeshi passport and national ID card through the high commission in New Delhi. A Bangladeshi court sentenced her to death in absentia in 2025 for crimes against humanity linked to a crackdown on student protesters. Dhaka says she has no further legal recourse after missing the deadline to appeal, that she would face execution if she returns, and it has sought her extradition from India, which says the request is under legal review. Hasina rejected the trial as illegitimate, denied that her Awami League was behind recent petrol bomb attacks, and said she faces more than 600 false cases and would not ask India for help to return. Analysts read the pledge as an effort to keep the banned Awami League relevant to its supporters, and it raises the risk of a fresh flashpoint between Dhaka and New Delhi.

stories.summary: Nearly 1,600 migrants reached Spain's Canary Islands on Saturday, most of them landing on the small island of El Hierro after a journey from West Africa. stories.headline: Hong Kong Rolls Out AI Facial Recognition Across CCTV Network
stories.claim: Hong Kong has rolled out AI facial recognition across its CCTV network as part of the SmartView police operation.
stories.summary: Hong Kong switched on AI-powered facial recognition across its camera network on Monday 16 November, widening surveillance of public spaces in the name of national security and crime prevention. The tools are part of the police SmartView operation and can monitor crowds, read licence plates and track criminal suspects. Police say about 5,000 CCTV cameras have been installed since SmartView launched in 2024, helping solve nearly 2,200 cases and make more than 2,800 arrests. Authorities plan to expand the network to 60,000 cameras by 2028. Critics worry about misuse of personal data, while police insist the system 'won't be abused'. The move extends the city's security reach since the 2019 protests and the national security law.

stories.headline: PM Burnham says Brexit has not worked as UK and EU prepare to sign food reset deal on Friday
stories.claim: PM Andy Burnham says Brexit 'has not worked' and will sign a reset deal with the EU at a summit on Friday.
stories.summary: Prime Minister Andy Burnham says Brexit "has not worked" and that he will sign a new agreement with the EU at a summit on Friday, in a speech to the Lord Mayor's Banquet in the City of London. He says the package could raise UK GDP by 0.4%, about £17bn, through food and farming, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme, and that any deal must meet Labour's manifesto, improve on current Brexit terms and pass his 'Makerfield test'. Relations minister Hamish Falconer said the UK would get a 'voice in the room' but no vote on EU food rules, with food-specific benefits worth an extra £5bn and lower paperwork and costs for exporters and eventually shoppers. An 'exit clause' may be included so a future government could not easily reverse closer alignment, a feature the EU wants because of the cost of its border checks. The Conservatives and Reform have both pledged to undo the reset if elected. The National Farmers' Union welcomed fewer checks but said farmers are waiting to see carve-outs and transitional arrangements, while Boris Johnson said Britain would 'absolutely' vote for Brexit again.

stories.headline: Apple launches Health AI Usage Study with OpenEvidence, seeking 200,000 US participants
stories.claim: Apple has launched a Health AI Usage Study with OpenEvidence, seeking up to 200,000 US adults to rate AI health answers.
stories.summary: Apple has launched the Apple Health AI Usage Study, a research programme run with the clinical AI platform OpenEvidence that asks members of the public to test AI health answers. Enrolment opened on Sunday through a new iOS app, and Apple is recruiting up to 200,000 participants. Those eligible must live in the US, be 21 or older and own an iPhone 15 Pro or later running iOS 26 or newer. Participants ask text-based health questions and rate the answers for accuracy, detail and relevance; the answers draw on peer-reviewed sources such as the New England Journal of Medicine and JAMA. The app does not use Siri or Apple Intelligence. Users may optionally share HealthKit data such as activity, sleep and lab results, and Apple says participant data stays confidential and will not be used to train AI models, though it may inform feature development. Participation can last up to 12 months, with surveys included. The study comes as about one in three US adults already use AI chatbots for health information, and it aims to shape how health AI tools are designed.

stories.claim: Plural, a European venture firm, has raised a new €1bn across two funds to back deep-tech start-ups.
stories.summary: Plural, the European venture firm founded in 2022, has raised €1 billion (about $1.1 billion) in new capital, one of the largest venture fundings in the region. Two thirds of the money will go into a third early-stage fund, while the remaining third backs a new "opportunities" fund for selective follow-on investments in its portfolio companies. stories.headline: SpaceX catches Starship upper stage with tower arms after Flight 15
stories.claim: SpaceX caught a Starship upper stage with the launch tower's chopstick arms at Starbase, Texas, the first ship capture after returning from orbit.
stories.summary: SpaceX caught a Starship upper stage with the mechanical 'chopstick' arms of its launch tower at Starbase in South Texas on Saturday, the first time a ship has been captured after returning from orbit. The spacecraft, about 170 feet long and travelling at more than 17,000 mph before re-entry, had launched on Friday at 5:47pm Eastern on its 15th test flight. It circled Earth 14 times and deployed 26 Starlink satellites, and SpaceX says its heat shield and other systems performed well. The planned double catch failed, however, because the 33-engine Super Heavy booster reported a guidance and navigation fault, was diverted into a simulated landing over the Gulf of Mexico and was destroyed there; the cause is still under investigation. SpaceX has caught boosters on three earlier flights, so the ship catch is the new milestone. Experts caution that heat shield and engine readiness for rapid reuse remain unproven, though full reusability could sharply cut launch costs. Musk said on the Q3 earnings call that a successful catch on the next flight was more likely than not. NASA relies on a Starship variant for its Artemis lunar lander, with Artemis III targeted for summer 2027, and SpaceX hopes to demonstrate orbital refuelling next year.

stories.headline: South Korea's top tax exam scorer confesses to AI-assisted cheating; exam glasses checks ordered
stories.claim: Han Won-seok, the top scorer on South Korea's tax accountancy exam, confessed on Sunday to cheating with a micro-camera and generative AI.
stories.summary: Han Won-seok, 34, the top scorer on South Korea's national certified tax accountancy exam, has confessed to cheating with a miniature camera, a mobile phone and generative AI tools. In a video posted on his lawyer's YouTube account on Sunday, he said he photographed exam questions, sent them to an AI tool and checked the answers on his phone, cheating in both rounds. He had scored 397.5 out of 400 in the first round, missing only one of 160 questions, which had triggered online suspicion. He has submitted a written confession to Seoul police, and the case has been assigned to investigators. The Ministry of Employment and Labour and the Human Resources Development Service held an emergency meeting, and the government says anyone found to have used AI will lose their qualification and be barred from retaking the test for five years. The scandal comes days before South Korea's national college entrance exam, where AI-glasses cheating has already prompted concern, and the government has promised tighter anti-cheating measures.

stories.headline: Gulf conflict energy shock set to drive next wave of food inflation, Rabobank warns

Banks are repricing mortgages and markets now expect the Bank of England to slow rate cuts. Rabobank argues the cushion that softened the 2021-22 shocks is largely gone, and that lower and middle-income shoppers will trade down, squeezing mid-tier brands the hardest.

stories.claim: Indian scientists have formally identified a new deep-sea bramble shark species, Echinorhinus roinee, off Kerala.
stories.summary: Indian scientists have formally named a new deep-sea shark species, Echinorhinus roinee, after specimens long mistaken for the Atlantic bramble shark were caught off India's south-western coast. The roughly three-metre animals, with thorn-like dermal denticles, had been landed at fishing harbours such as Sakthikulangara in Kerala for years. Researchers from the Zoological Survey of India and the ICAR-Central Marine Fisheries Research Institute found anatomical differences, and DNA analysis showed the Indian sharks form a distinct evolutionary lineage separate from both the Atlantic and Pacific bramble sharks. Very little is known about the species' biology, but bramble sharks are generally thought to grow slowly and mature late, which makes the discovery a reminder of how much of the deep ocean remains poorly studied.

stories.claim: Spain holds a snap general election on 29 November, with polls pointing to the PP falling short of a majority and needing Vox.
stories.summary: Spaniards vote on 29 November in a snap general election, the sixth in eleven years, which could bring the far right into government for the first time since Franco's death. Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez called the vote on 5 October after the conservative PP, Vox and Junts blocked his emergency housing measures. Polls suggest the PP will finish first with about 130 of 350 seats, short of the 176 needed for a majority, while the PSOE trails on about 110 and Vox could win around 63. A PP-Vox deal would therefore be the likely route to government, and the two already govern four regions together. The campaign is also shaped by a housing crisis, a fatal high-speed rail crash and corruption allegations against the government.

He described sheltering in churches through nights of heavy Russian attacks and seeing hundreds of buildings levelled. He also recounted rescuing wounded soldiers from a roadside after their car was hit by a rocket earlier this month. Masters, who has made 14 trips since the war began and fundraises through a Hereford cafe, returned home at the end of last week. stories.summary: UK blood services have launched an urgent appeal for 150,000 donations as winter approaches, with some blood types at half the level considered necessary. Reserves of O negative, B negative, O positive and R0 blood are particularly low, and officials want 5,000 donors a day until the new year. Winter illness keeps some people from giving blood while those with long-term conditions such as sickle cell disease and cancer need more transfusions. Scotland has already issued its first amber alert for O blood types after stocks fell to unprecedented lows. Each donation takes about an hour and can help save three lives.

stories.headline: Fashion Sourcing Is Big Business. Luxury Is Catching On.
stories.claim: Italian court placed Loro Piana under 12-month judicial administration over worker exploitation in its supply chain.
stories.summary: Loro Piana, the Italian cashmere house owned by LVMH, was placed under a 12-month court administration last week over alleged worker exploitation in its supply chain. Milanese prosecutors found that a Chinese-run subcontractor passed cashmere jacket work to illegal workshops on the outskirts of Milan, where ten workers, five of them undocumented, were reportedly forced to work up to 90 hours a week for as little as €4 an hour. The brand is not under criminal investigation, and the order can be lifted if it meets legal requirements before the deadline. Loro Piana says it cut ties with the supplier within 24 hours of being alerted on 20 May. It is the fifth Italian fashion house placed under court monitoring since 2023, after Armani and Dior, which were both released early in February. The case deepens scrutiny of the Made in Italy label.

stories.summary: Helena Rosol, now 93 and living in a care home in Fortrose in the Scottish Highlands, has been awarded Poland's Siberian Exiles Cross for the hardships she endured as a child in the Second World War. Deported with her family to Siberia in February 1940 when she was about six, she lost almost all her relatives in forced labour camps. Her father survived but died on the journey out of Russia. Her route later took her through Kazakhstan, Iran and Afghanistan to an orphanage in India, and eventually to England. The honour was arranged after her husband contacted the Polish embassy. stories.headline: ‘It’s like the 16th-century version of doomscrolling’: the Book of Miracles may fetch £1m at auction
stories.claim: Christie's will auction the only known copy of the 16th-century Book of Miracles in London on 10 December, estimated at £700,000-£1m.
stories.summary: A rare 16th-century German 'wonderbook' called the Book of Miracles, which holds 167 painted scenes of apocalyptic visions and extreme weather, is expected to fetch £700,000 to £1m at Christie's in London on 10 December. It is the only known copy and was made in Augsburg in the 1550s, but scholars only learned of it after it turned up in a German castle library almost 20 years ago. It sold in 2008 for just over £100,000 and later entered the collection of Connecticut collector Mickey Cartin. Christie's says the watercolour and gouache scenes look strikingly modern, and the auction house is offering public institutions the first chance to bid. The sale is a rare chance to see an unusual piece of early science and culture reporting.
key_points: The Book of Miracles contains 167 paintings of apocalyptic visions, celestial wonders and extreme weather, made in mid-16th century Augsburg.

Public institutions get the first chance to bid, and the public can view it for six days before the sale.

stories.headline: Is an autism or ADHD diagnosis key to helping people?
stories.claim: NHS is steering people away from formal autism and ADHD diagnoses toward quicker targeted help, as waits exceed seven years.
stories.summary: More than 1.25 million people in England are waiting for autism or ADHD diagnosis or treatment, with waits of more than seven years in some cases. A major government-commissioned review led by Prof Peter Fonagy, published in October, found monthly ADHD assessment referrals rose from about 5,000 in 2019 to about 17,000. The panel said the system now risks misdiagnosis and overdiagnosis but could not conclude overdiagnosis is happening at scale, pointing instead to greater awareness and reduced stigma. It said the system leans too heavily on diagnosis as the route to help. Three NHS organisations in north-west England are piloting routes for children that do not depend on a clinical diagnosis.

stories.headline: Explainer: What is the polar vortex and what could it mean for winter?
stories.claim: The Arctic polar vortex is weakening unusually early this year, which could raise the risk of a colder winter in Europe and North America.
stories.summary: The Arctic polar vortex, the ring of strong winds that normally keeps frigid air over the North Pole, is weakening unusually early this November. Meteorologists say this does not guarantee a harsh winter, but it could increase the chance of cold, dry conditions across parts of the Northern Hemisphere later in the season. Adam Scaife of the Met Office said there have been collapses in November before but never this early in the month. Scientists are still investigating, with possible links to unusually warm Arctic ocean temperatures and an exceptionally strong El Niño developing this year. Such disruptions usually bring cold air into Europe and North America a week or two after the upper-atmosphere change.
key_points: The stratospheric polar vortex is weakening earlier than usual, which meteorologists say is unusual.
Sudden stratospheric warming is one of the main causes of such disruptions.

The current rules require 80% of new car sales to be electric from 2030 and 100% from 2035, but reports suggest Labour is preparing to lower these targets. Campaigners argue a slower EV market would keep running costs high, noting a petrol fill-up can cost over £100 while a full EV charge is under £10. stories.headline: ‘Prove you are not a robot’: how the Captcha scam captures your computer

stories.summary: A scam known as ClickFix is becoming one of the most common ways criminals infect people's computers with malware, according to Malwarebytes researcher Chris Fistonich. Instead of the familiar image or letter Captcha, victims are told to press keys such as Windows Key plus R, then Ctrl plus V and Enter. This copies malicious code into the clipboard and runs it on the device. The scam is especially effective during the Christmas shopping season, when people visit unfamiliar small-business websites. Fistonich says people are not prepared for it because they trust Captchas and security software. Advice includes pausing before following any on-screen instructions, using security software that blocks malicious sites, and, if compromised, contacting the bank and changing passwords.

stories.summary: Reports of artificial intelligence being used to sexually exploit children have risen by more than 8,400% in two years, according to new research from Edinburgh-based Childlight. AI-related abuse material, including deepfakes made with "nudify" apps, rose from about 4,700 cases in 2023 to more than 400,000 in 2025. The data comes from reports filed by tech companies with the US National Center for Missing and Exploited Children. Childlight says better detection may explain part of the jump, but calls it an extraordinary rise. Separately, the Internet Watch Foundation found 6,310 AI images meeting the legal definition of child sexual abuse in the first half of 2026, 40% above last year's total. Childlight estimates over 300 million children worldwide suffer technology-facilitated sexual exploitation each year and calls on governments to treat the problem as a preventable public health emergency.

It returned earlier than the four-week restoration it had promised, on Sunday, with some features such as importing external works and icons still disabled. Works can only be downloaded as HTML for now. The nonprofit Organization for Transformative Works says no works, bookmarks or kudos were deleted and it has no reason to believe the user database was compromised, though it cannot rule this out. Traffic surges caused loading delays, which the site said were deliberate. Draft deletion resumes on 29 November, when drafts older than 30 days will be removed.

stories.headline: UK exposed to polycrisis of threats amid government ‘complacency’
stories.claim: A House of Lords committee says UK ministers are complacent and unprepared for interconnected threats, and urges a national resilience overhaul.
stories.summary: A Lords committee has warned that the UK government is complacent and underprepared for a 'polycrisis' of linked threats, from cyber-attacks and sabotage to extreme weather. The report, written after months of expert hearings, calls for a dedicated cabinet minister, an annual prime ministerial statement on preparedness, and a booklet for every household like those in Denmark and Sweden. It highlights fragile supply chains: about 90% of the world's 6-APA, the basis of penicillin-type antibiotics, comes from China, and the UK has no integrated penicillin facility. Nearly 95% of UK retail food is supplied by nine companies. BT has just two cable repair ships, one of them 35 years old. The Cabinet Office said it would review the recommendations and pointed to its £1bn-plus investment in pandemic security.
key_points: A House of Lords national resilience committee says ministers are complacent and the UK is underprepared for linked crises.
It recommends a dedicated cabinet minister and an annual prime ministerial statement on preparedness.
It urges a household preparedness booklet and a pause to plans to switch off digital terrestrial TV.
About 90% of the world's 6-APA, used in penicillin-type antibiotics, comes from China, and the UK has no integrated penicillin plant.
Nearly 95% of UK retail food is supplied by nine companies from 131 distribution hubs.
The Cabinet Office says it will review the recommendations and points to over £1bn invested in pandemic security.

stories.headline: A timber bridge leads the way into this Nova Scotia coastal retreat
stories.claim: RHAD Architects completes Bridge House, a cedar-clad timber holiday retreat on Nova Scotia's South Shore reached by a footbridge.
stories.summary: A holiday home on Nova Scotia's South Shore arrives at its front door by a timber footbridge, a deliberate piece of theatre designed to heighten the sense of arrival. Bridge House, by Dartmouth-based RHAD Architects, is set back on its plot so it cannot be seen from the street, and visitors drive along a path to a parking court before crossing the bridge into the first floor. The entry sequence includes a sheltered outdoor area and a mudroom built for heavy Canadian winter gear. The main living spaces, including kitchen and dining, sit on the piano nobile beneath a double-height hall with a glazed front facing the cove, while bedrooms are upstairs linked by an internal bridge. The cedar-clad volume draws on local boathouses and cabins, and the architects frame it as both rooted in the coast's traditions and contemporary in its response to climate.
key_points: RHAD Architects, based in Dartmouth, designed Bridge House as a holiday retreat on Nova Scotia's South Shore.
The home is set back from the street for privacy, approached by a driveway and a timber footbridge.
The footbridge is described by the architects as a ceremonial threshold between landscape and architecture.
Living spaces sit on the first floor under a double-height glazed hall facing the cove; bedrooms are upstairs.
The cedar-clad form takes cues from local boathouses and cabins and the coast's vernacular architecture.

stories.headline: 2026 Record Awards Winner: La Source Vive by PCA-Stream
stories.claim: La Source Vive, a 490-seat copper-clad chamber music hall in Évian-les-Bains, France, wins the 2026 Record Architecture award.
stories.summary: A chamber music hall in the French spa town of Évian-les-Bains has been named a 2026 Record Awards winner by Architectural Record. La Source Vive seats 490 people and is tucked into a wooded dell beside an existing 1,000-seat concert hall by the same architect, Patrick Bouchain. Designed with Philippe Chiambaretta of PCA-Stream, it has a 10-inch concrete shell, a separate glulam dome with a 6-foot gap, and an exterior of hand-bent burnished copper leaves, a technique borrowed from the region's onion-domed churches. An electronically operated blind adapted from sailboat technology can black out the top oculus. The building is a showcase of collaboration between architects, acousticians and builders.
key_points: La Source Vive is a 490-seat chamber music venue in Évian-les-Bains, France.
It was designed by Patrick Bouchain and Philippe Chiambaretta of PCA-Stream.

stories.headline: Tant A Temps Design "restores the visual characteristics of Tang architecture" in Chinese cafe
stories.claim: Tant A Temps Design has fitted out the Laibei 1087 cafe inside a Song-era stele museum in Xi'an, China, with reversible, Tang-inspired interiors.
stories.summary: Inside a building dating to 1087 in Xi'an, China, a new café uses a reversible, Tang-inspired design that avoids touching the historic structure. Laibei 1087 sits in the Beilin Museum, built to house stone steles inscribed with Confucian texts and calligraphy. Interior practice Tant A Temps Design, led by founder Wei Chen, followed a minimum-intervention approach: furniture hangs from beams or stands around columns, and new elements are detachable. The bar counter hides all modern services such as air conditioning, plumbing and electrics. The 220-square-metre project includes a rest area, a retail zone and a stone-rubbing workshop, and the studio presents it as a model for adaptive reuse of heritage buildings.

Tant A Temps Design, led by Wei Chen, designed the interiors using a zero-damage, reversible strategy.

stories.headline: Olivia von Halle wants you to wear your pyjamas out
stories.claim: London designer Olivia von Halle reflects on 15 years of her pyjama-inspired label and its new Aari-embroidered Resort 2027 collection.
stories.summary: London-based designer Olivia von Halle, who founded her eponymous label in 2011 during London Fashion Week, has built a luxury brand from silk pyjamas she first had made by a tailor in Shanghai. The brand now sells through Harrods, Selfridges, Le Bon Marché and Net-a-Porter, and has dressed figures such as Victoria Beckham, the Hadid sisters and Angelina Jolie. Her recently revealed Resort 2027 collection features Aari embroidery by Indian artisans, with each motif taking around half an hour of handwork. The interview frames a wider shift in which pyjama-style pieces move into daywear, a trend seen at Prada and Dolce & Gabbana. The story is a profile rather than a business announcement, but it shows how bedwear-led luxury is gaining ground.

stories.headline: Israel says it killed senior Hamas commander Samir Abu Younis; Hamas confirms
stories.claim: Israel says it killed senior Hamas commander Samir Abu Younis in a Khan Younis strike; Hamas confirms his death.
stories.summary: Hamas's Al-Qassam Brigades has confirmed that Samir Abu Younis, 53, commander of its Rafah Brigade, was killed in an Israeli airstrike on Saturday evening in Al-Mawasi, Khan Younis, in southern Gaza. Israel's military and Shin Bet said in a joint statement that they had struck Abu Younis, a senior Hamas military wing figure who helped plan the 7 October 2023 attack. Hamas said he had joined its armed wing in 1991 and called the strike a cowardly assassination, and Gaza's civil defence said it received his body and that two people were wounded. The strike tests the October 2025 US-backed ceasefire, which both sides accuse each other of violating and which has not halted Israeli strikes or secured Hamas disarmament. Gaza health authorities say at least 1,600 Palestinians have died since the truce took effect, and five Israeli soldiers have been killed in the same period. The killing comes as Israel's caretaker prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu remains responsible for military operations while rival Gadi Eisenkot negotiates a coalition.

stories.claim: Britain rejoins Erasmus+ from January 2027 at a cost of £570m in year one, with Jean Monnet funding criticised as EU propaganda.
stories.summary: Britain will rejoin the EU's Erasmus+ student exchange scheme from January 2027, at a cost of £570m for its first year, under a deal agreed with Brussels. The Telegraph reports that the scheme will also fund Jean Monnet actions, which universities and teacher-training programmes can apply for, prompting Conservative and Reform UK critics to call it EU propaganda. Four British universities have applied for Jean Monnet funding this year. Ongoing costs could rise sharply, since Brussels plans to increase the scheme's 2028-34 budget by more than 50 per cent, to around €26bn–€41bn. Labour has not yet said whether membership will continue beyond the first year, and the row feeds into the government's wider EU reset.

stories.summary: Lanvin Group, the Shanghai- and Milan-based luxury fashion company behind Lanvin, Wolford, Sergio Rossi and St. John Knits, has received a continued listing notice from the New York Stock Exchange. stories.headline: Microsoft 365 global outage over; services fully restored after day-long disruption
stories.claim: Microsoft says Microsoft 365 is fully restored after a global outage of more than 24 hours that began on 12 November, with no evidence of cyberattack.
stories.summary: Microsoft confirmed on Saturday 14 November that Microsoft 365 services were restored for all remaining customers and regions after an outage lasting more than 24 hours. The disruption hit Outlook, Teams, Copilot and other apps used by businesses and governments worldwide, and Downdetector logged more than 7.4 million outage reports. The problem began with Exchange Online at 11:17am ET on 12 November, with a wider Microsoft 365 failure two hours later. Microsoft first suspected heavy traffic, then found several backend servers had become unavailable. It traced the root cause to an earlier network capacity upgrade that was exposed by a later network change, and deployed a patch for an authentication and routing component. Microsoft found no evidence of malicious activity and said AI was not the cause. In the UK, NHS England hospitals reverted to paper records and ambulance services reported serious impact, while courts and schools were affected; Australian agencies, Air India and IndiGo were also hit. The outage has renewed concern about dependence on a few large cloud providers.
key_points: Microsoft confirmed on Saturday 14 November that services were restored for all remaining customers and regions.
The outage began with Exchange Online at 11:17am ET on 12 November, with a wider Microsoft 365 failure at 1:26pm ET.
Root cause was traced to an earlier network capacity upgrade that was exposed by a subsequent network change.
Microsoft found no evidence of malicious activity and said AI was not the cause.
NHS England hospitals reverted to paper records, and courts, councils, Australian agencies and airlines were affected.
Downdetector recorded over 7.4 million outage reports worldwide, though that is not a count of individual users.
stories.market_take: Limited direct market effect; the outage highlights cloud concentration risk for Microsoft's enterprise business.

stories.headline: UK government to consider changing age of consent after Russell Brand accuser's call
stories.claim: UK government will consider changing the age of consent after Mia Latter alleged Russell Brand raped her at 16; the Met investigation continues.
stories.summary: Deputy Prime Minister Louise Haigh said the government will consider changing the age of consent after Mia Latter, one of six women who accused Russell Brand in a 2023 investigation, publicly alleged he raped her when she was 16 and he was 30. Latter, now 37, has waived her anonymity to campaign for a "staggered" age of consent that would make relationships between adults and 16- and 17-year-olds an offence. Haigh said the proposal was a massive step that deserved proper scrutiny, and equalities minister Bridget Phillipson praised her courage, while Liberal Democrat justice spokesperson Jess Brown-Fuller backed reviewing the law. Under current UK law, adults of any age can legally have sex with 16- and 17-year-olds. The Met Police opened its investigation into Latter's allegation in January 2026 and says it remains ongoing, with further information needed before a charging decision. Latter says she will not pursue the criminal process so she can focus on her campaign. Brand was sentenced to 10.5 years for one rape and three sexual assaults, though none of the 2023 accusers were complainants in that trial. Haigh also floated banning NDAs in harassment cases, following reports that an accuser of David Walliams was asked to sign one.
key_points: Deputy Prime Minister Louise Haigh said the government will consider changing the age of consent.
Mia Latter, 37, waived her anonymity and alleges Brand raped her when she was 16 and he was 30.
Latter is campaigning for a staggered age of consent that would criminalise adult relationships with 16- and 17-year-olds.
The Met Police opened its investigation in January 2026 and says it remains ongoing.
Brand was sentenced to 10.5 years for one rape and three sexual assault counts in a separate trial.
Haigh suggested banning NDAs in harassment cases after reports that a Walliams accuser was asked to sign one.

stories.headline: Philippines and Australia sign defence pact to speed joint military activity amid China concerns
stories.claim: Philippines and Australia signed a defence cooperation arrangement in Manila on Sunday to cut bureaucracy slowing joint military activity.
stories.summary: The Philippines and Australia signed a defence cooperation arrangement in Manila on Sunday, 15 November, designed to cut the bureaucracy that slows joint military activity. Philippine Defence Secretary Gilberto Teodoro said the process of implementing the existing Status of Visiting Forces Agreement would shrink from about 100 steps to roughly 10. The deal opens the way for closer cooperation across maritime, air and land forces, as well as humanitarian and disaster response, and is framed as strengthening deterrence in the South China Sea. Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, attending an ASEAN summit in Manila, witnessed the signing and announced extra Australian investment in maritime surveillance, including drone technology, equipment and training. Beijing routinely opposes such drills, saying they raise regional tensions, and the pact adds to a growing network of security partnerships among US allies in the region.

stories.headline: COP31 nations split over keeping 1.5C target as UN says it will be missed
stories.claim: At COP31 in Antalya, negotiators are split over whether the final deal should keep the 1.5C goal, as the UN says crossing it is imminent.
stories.summary: Negotiators at the COP31 UN climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye, are divided over whether to keep the 1.5C warming limit, which the UN said in September is imminent and effectively unavoidable. The world has already warmed about 1.4C above pre-industrial levels. Palau's president Surangel Whipps Jr called 1.5C an existential threat, and frontline states want the final deal to affirm it as the right goal and return to it as soon as possible. According to AFP observers, the Arab Group and Like-Minded Developing Countries, including Saudi Arabia and India, see room to drop the target, partly fearing pressure to cut emissions without extra finance. Australia, which is chairing the negotiations, has released a summary of negotiating positions as the talks reach their midway point. Outgoing UN chief Antonio Guterres said any overshoot must be as small and brief as possible. Scientists warn that weakening the target could slow the emissions cuts needed to limit floods, heatwaves and coral loss, and Exeter's Pierre Friedlingstein said returning to 1.5C would require a massive, decades-long roll-out of carbon removal.
key_points: The UN said in September that crossing 1.5C is imminent and effectively unavoidable, with the world already about 1.4C warmer.

stories.headline: Zelensky says US floated Donbas-for-NATO deal and accuses SpaceX over Starshield
stories.claim: Zelensky says US envoys floated Ukraine ceding Donbas in exchange for NATO membership; Kyiv refuses and the US has not confirmed it.
stories.summary: Volodymyr Zelensky says US negotiators asked whether Ukraine would withdraw from the parts of eastern Donbas that Russia does not control in exchange for NATO membership, a question he says had never been raised before. He said Kyiv is not ready to concede territory, though it would put any concrete proposal to a national referendum if it came with security guarantees, a strong funded army and reconstruction money. Neither Washington nor NATO has publicly confirmed the idea, and a US official said many ideas are under discussion. Jared Kushner later urged confidentiality and called some reported proposals maximalist, which was read as a rebuke to Kyiv. Earlier, Zelensky accused SpaceX of lying about speed limits on Starshield, saying Ukrainian drones had been capped at 161km/h for five days, which he called political rather than technical. Russia has not shifted its position and still demands territorial concessions and limits on Ukraine's army, including Ukraine ceding the rest of Donbas and Crimea before any ceasefire.

stories.headline: Andy Burnham says UK has ‘lost more than we gained’ through Brexit
stories.claim: PM Andy Burnham says UK has lost more than it gained from Brexit and plans a food and farming deal with the EU.
stories.summary: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said the UK has lost more than it has gained since leaving the EU, blaming the Conservatives for burning bridges with Brussels. Speaking at the Welsh Labour conference, he said a deal he hopes to secure at a UK-EU summit next week could raise GDP by 0.4 per cent, about £17bn, through agreements on food and farming, emissions trading and youth mobility. He says the deal would lower food prices and help exporters. Burnham has said he is open to rejoining the single market or customs union, but insists on Labour's manifesto red lines that rule those out. EU leaders will meet him in Brussels on 20 November, where deals could be signed, though Brussels has said the UK must pay to access EU programmes and cannot cherry-pick.
key_points: Burnham said the UK has lost more than it gained over the past decade and blamed the Conservatives for a harsh Brexit.
The UK-EU agreements are estimated to add 0.4 per cent to GDP, about £17bn.
Planned deals cover food and farming, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme.
Burnham reaffirmed Labour's red lines against rejoining the customs union, single market or free movement.

stories.headline: Copa jet and UPS plane collide on Miami airport taxiway
stories.claim: A Copa Airlines Boeing 737 and a UPS Boeing 767 collided while taxiing at Miami International Airport on Saturday evening.
stories.summary: A Copa Airlines Boeing 737 and a UPS Boeing 767 collided while taxiing at Miami International Airport on Saturday around 9:15pm local time. The Copa jet's wingtip struck the nose of the UPS freighter, which was heading to Bogota, Colombia. The FAA said air traffic controllers had told the UPS crew to give way. Two people were treated at the scene for minor injuries and did not need hospital care. Flights were diverted to other taxiways, so airport operations were not disrupted. The incident is a ground accident with no reported major damage.

stories.headline: Iran Attacks Bahrain as Conflict Escalates
stories.claim: US and Iranian forces escalated strikes, with Iran hitting US bases in Bahrain, Jordan, Iraq and Kuwait.
stories.summary: The US and Iran have escalated their conflict, with a new wave of American strikes on southern Iran prompting Iranian missile and drone attacks on US bases in Bahrain, Jordan, Iraq and Kuwait. CENTCOM says it hit air defences, radar and mine-laying assets after Revolutionary Guard attempts to attack shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. Kuwait suspended operations at its international airport, and Iran's energy ministry asked citizens to cut power use after strikes on the grid, with the strikes now a seventh consecutive night. stories.headline: Italy fines Meta €805m over accessing Android users' photos
stories.claim: Italy's data regulator fined Meta €805m (about $887m) over Facebook's Android photo-access feature, and Meta says it will appeal.
stories.summary: Italy's data protection authority, the Garante, has fined Meta €805 million (about $887 million), its largest penalty ever, for the Facebook Android app's access to users' photos and videos without specific consent. The regulator said about 20 million Italian Android users were affected by the camera-roll gallery suggestions feature, which has run since 2023. It found that a single app-wide permission covered several features and was presented with a vague warning, and it cited Meta's lack of cooperation during the investigation. The Garante used ePrivacy rules to sidestep the one-stop-shop system that would normally send the case to Ireland, where Meta's EU base sits, rejecting Meta's argument. Meta must obtain separate consent within 60 days, explain the feature clearly and make it off by default, including for existing users. The fine equals roughly 0.4% of Meta's 2025 turnover of $201bn. Meta says it strongly disagrees, will appeal and argues the permission can be changed at any time. The penalty follows a $25bn New Mexico judgment against the company last month. A separate look at a 2026 cloud feature is planned.
key_points: Italy's Garante fined Meta €805m (about $887m), the largest fine it has ever imposed.
About 20 million Italian Android users were affected by the gallery suggestions feature launched in 2023.

stories.market_take: The fine is small relative to Meta's profits, so the direct share price impact is likely minimal.

stories.headline: Passengers face widespread disruption after US air traffic control outage
stories.claim: An air traffic control technical fault disrupted UK flights at Heathrow, Gatwick and other airports on Tuesday and Wednesday.
stories.summary: A technical fault at Nats, the UK's air traffic control provider, caused hundreds of thousands of passengers to face cancellations and delays across Tuesday and Wednesday. Heathrow, Gatwick, Luton and Glasgow were among the main airports affected, with stranded travellers reporting sleeping in terminals and chaotic baggage halls. Nats says operations are now stable, though airlines warn of knock-on disruption for days. Nats chief executive Martin Rolfe has apologised, and Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander has asked for a full investigation. The Financial Times notes the political blame game is intensifying, with thousands of flights hit. The episode raises questions about the resilience of the UK's air traffic system.

stories.headline: Anthropic IPO: pricing set for Nov 18 at up to $1.4tn, with investor and rival scrutiny
stories.claim: Anthropic has filed to offer 825 million shares at $70-$78 each, with pricing set for 18 November and trading to start the next day.
stories.summary: Anthropic is preparing a Nasdaq listing that could value the AI company at up to about $1.4 trillion, one of the largest IPOs ever. Its updated filing offers 825 million shares priced between $70 and $78 each, and at the top of the range the sale would raise $64.35 billion. Pricing is planned for 18 November, with trading under the ticker ANT starting the following day. Earlier filings showed the seven founders, led by CEO Dario Amodei, planning to sell about $250 million each, and reports say the founders hold about 50.1% of most votes despite owning roughly 22% of shares. A separate $26 billion private placement involving Nvidia and Alphabet sits outside the public offering and could push total capital raised above SpaceX's June IPO. Reports that several banks have turned away buy orders from mainland Chinese and Hong Kong investors, citing ITAR export rules, could narrow the investor base. Anthropic reported $33.2 billion in revenue for the first nine months of 2026, up 1,206% year on year, and reports suggest the offering is heavily oversubscribed and underwriters may price above the range.

stories.headline: Google turned to AMD Epyc, not its own Axion chips, to secure its first confidential TPU
stories.claim: Google's eighth-generation TPU 8tx for confidential AI uses AMD Epyc CPUs rather than its own Axion chips.
stories.summary: Google has added the TPU 8tx to its eighth-generation TPU family, a system for confidential AI that pairs its accelerator with AMD's 5th Gen Epyc CPUs rather than its own Axion chips. Google says the 8tx offers up to 2x lower latency than the TPU 8t, and is aimed at regulated enterprises and governments that want to train models on private data. AMD says its Secure Encrypted Virtualization extends protection to the accelerators, a first for cloud TPUs. The 8tx reuses existing chips rather than new designs, and Google reportedly chose Turin to match PCIe Gen5 interfaces. AMD shares closed up 13.26% at $508.58 on 9 November, though the move also reflected other factors. Analysts see the deal as a sign of closer ties, but not a confirmed accelerator partnership.
key_points: Google's TPU 8tx is a system configuration that pairs its accelerator with AMD 5th Gen Epyc CPUs for confidential computing.
AMD says Epyc with SEV extends hardware-enforced protection to TPU accelerators, described as a first in cloud TPUs.

stories.headline: EU leaders pick five-nation group to represent Europe in Ukraine peace talks at Dublin summit
stories.claim: EU leaders agreed at the Dublin summit that Europe's representatives in Ukraine peace talks will be the E5 powers plus the Commission and Council.
stories.summary: EU leaders agreed at a summit in Dublin that Europe's representatives in future Ukraine peace talks will be national security officials from Germany, France, the UK, Italy and Poland, the so-called E5, together with the European Commission and European Council. The arrangement was added to the agenda at the last minute at Giorgia Meloni's request, ending months of disagreement over who should speak for the bloc. It followed concern about a possible Yalta-style arrangement after a Trump-Putin meeting set for 18-19 November at the APEC summit in Shenzhen. Putin said he was open to Europeans joining talks, but Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov attached conditions, which Kaja Kallas dismissed as a trap. Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin said the choice needed to be settled within a week or two, while Macron stressed that Europe must define its own security. The move gives Europe a clearer negotiating voice as Washington, Moscow and Kyiv negotiate, and Russia has objected to European involvement.
key_points: EU leaders agreed Europe's representatives in future Ukraine talks will be the E5 powers plus the Commission and Council.
The E5 comprises Germany, France, the UK, Italy and Poland, and the arrangement was added at Giorgia Meloni's request.
A Trump-Putin meeting is set for 18-19 November at the APEC summit in Shenzhen, which alarmed European capitals.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov attached conditions to European participation, which Kaja Kallas dismissed as a trap.
Earlier, Zelenskyy had pressed for Europe to become a regular part of talks, which ended in Abu Dhabi without a breakthrough.
Europe's first-hand voice in talks is intended to counter fears of being sidelined.

stories.headline: Tanker strikes docked American Heritage cruise ship in New Orleans; port sues owners
stories.claim: A loaded tanker struck the docked American Heritage cruise ship in New Orleans; the Port of New Orleans has sued the tanker's owners.
stories.summary: The Port of New Orleans sued the owners and managers of the tanker Atlantic Asphalt on Saturday, seeking more than $1m and asking that the vessel be seized and sold. The suit names Nave Shipping SA, a subsidiary of China State Shipbuilding Corporation, and manager Thome Ship Management, and was filed in federal court in the Eastern District of Louisiana. The loaded tanker struck the docked American Heritage, a American Cruise Lines paddlewheel river ship, on the Mississippi at about 12:30pm on Friday, causing it to tilt and partly take on water. The ship had 197 passengers aboard, and 32 people were taken to hospital, mostly with bumps and bruises, including two harbour police officers. New Orleans' mayor called it a 'miracle on the Mississippi' because no one was killed or critically hurt. The Coast Guard said the tanker apparently lost steering, though the cause is under investigation. Many passengers lost IDs, phones and belongings, and the city is providing food, hotels and transport.

stories.headline: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO over affair with suspected Chinese spy; Kress interim CEO
stories.claim: Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO on 12 November over an affair; CFO Colette Kress is interim CEO and Huang is reportedly weighing a comeback.
stories.summary: Nvidia's stock was rattled further this week as Bessent demanded a shakeup and an outside successor. Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's president, CEO and board member with immediate effect on Thursday 12 November after admitting extramarital affairs, one reportedly with Alice Huang, a Singapore-based executive whom US officials suspect was recruited by China's Ministry of State Security; Beijing calls the spy claims a smear. Chief financial officer Colette Kress, at Nvidia since 2013, is interim chief executive while the board searches for a permanent successor, and longtime director Harvey Jones became the company's first independent chair. Nvidia shares fell as much as 14% in early trading on Friday before closing down just over 4%, and roughly $1 trillion of market value has been wiped out this month. The Financial Times reported that Huang is discussing a return, with allies including Elon Musk building a support campaign, while a petition had gathered more than 115,000 signatures. Nvidia may lack full insurance cover for executive conduct, raising lawsuit risk, and the company reports its first quarterly results without Huang on 17 November.
key_points: Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia president, CEO and board member with immediate effect on 12 November.
Colette Kress, CFO since 2013, is interim CEO while the board searches for a permanent successor.
Harvey Jones became Nvidia's first independent chair.
Shares fell as much as 14% early Friday and closed down just over 4%; roughly $1 trillion of value has been lost this month.
The FT reported Huang is discussing a return, and a petition has over 115,000 signatures urging his reinstatement.
Nvidia reports first quarterly results without Huang on 17 November.
signals: Company says it has not formally engaged any candidates
Single original report cited by other outlets

stories.headline: FAA lifts nationwide ground stop caused by copper-to-fibre upgrade failure
stories.claim: The FAA lifted a rare nationwide ground stop on Friday evening after nearly five hours, blamed on a telecom failure during copper-to-fibre work; recovery is expected before Thanksgiving.
stories.summary: The FAA lifted a rare nationwide ground stop at about 8.15pm Eastern on Friday, ending nearly five hours of disruption that halted US departures. Officials blamed a telecommunications failure during routine work replacing old copper lines with fibre at a remote FAA facility, and said there was no sign of a cyberattack. Transport Secretary Sean Duffy said a newly installed router flooded other air traffic control routers with more than 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, disrupting radar feeds and communications with aircraft, while the root cause, possibly faulty hardware, a misconfigured router or contractor error by L3Harris, remains under investigation. More than 6,700 flights were cancelled on Friday and over 25,000 delayed, according to FlightAware, and JetBlue cancelled all domestic flights. Cancellations continued into the weekend, with more than 6,000 on Saturday, and about 4,000 aircraft that were airborne all landed safely. About 1.5 million travellers were affected, according to House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries. Duffy has pressed Congress for $30 billion, later saying up to $50 billion, to modernise the air traffic control system, and normal operations are expected before Thanksgiving on 26 November.
key_points: The FAA lifted the first nationwide ground stop since January 2023 at about 8.15pm Eastern on Friday, after nearly five hours.
Transport Secretary Sean Duffy said a newly installed router flooded other air traffic control routers with over 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds.
More than 6,700 flights were cancelled on Friday and over 25,000 delayed, with JetBlue cancelling all domestic flights.
Cancellations continued with more than 6,000 on Saturday, and normal schedules are not expected until late Sunday.
About 1.5 million travellers were affected, according to House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries.
Duffy has asked Congress for $30 billion, later saying up to $50 billion, to modernise air traffic control; L3Harris has completed more than 70% of the planned conversion.

stories.headline: European shares end best week since June as strong earnings lift sentiment
stories.claim: European shares had their best week since June, with the STOXX 600 flat on Friday but up over 2% for the week.
stories.summary: European shares finished their best week since late June, with the STOXX 600 closing flat at 664.14 points on Friday but up more than 2% over the week. The Euro STOXX banks index rose over 4% and led the gains. Strong earnings, a fall in oil prices on hopes of easing US-Iran tensions, and a rotation out of tech helped the index touch record highs on Thursday for the first time since August. Tech stocks fell 1.3% on Friday after Nvidia's chief executive Jensen Huang abruptly resigned, with chip stocks such as Infineon and Aixtron down more than 4%. Richemont fell 3.8% after weaker jewellery sales, and Acciona dropped 8% after its energy unit said it would miss an asset rotation target. Goldman Sachs raised its 12-month STOXX 600 target to 700 from 695.

stories.headline: Researchers say Chinese AI models were trained on banned Nvidia Blackwell GPUs
stories.claim: Independent researchers claim Chinese open-weight AI models show fingerprints of training on Nvidia Blackwell GPUs banned for China; the claim is unreviewed.
stories.summary: Independent researchers, including former OpenAI engineer Will DePue through his consultancy Unemployment Labs, claim several Chinese AI models were trained on Nvidia's Blackwell GPUs, which US export controls restrict for China. The team says it matched weight-initialisation patterns of open-weight models against more than six trillion chip and seed combinations, finding conclusive evidence for six models, including DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Kimi K3.1 and MiniMax-M3, with Ling-3.1-Flash also named. The team says AMD cards did not match the weight pattern for DeepSeek V4. The analysis has not been peer reviewed, and the researchers stress that it identifies the chip type only, not where the chips were physically located, how they were accessed, or whether any export rule was broken. Renting Blackwell hardware abroad, including from US cloud providers, is not clearly illegal, and the method works only on open-weight models. The claims arrive as several bills pending in Congress seek to tighten chip export rules, and they bear on Nvidia's China exposure and on enforcement of export controls.

Dark matter makes up about 27% of the universe and remains undetected directly, with candidates including neutrinos, WIMPs and primordial black holes. stories.headline: Nine-day Brighton Main Line closure warning
stories.claim: Brighton Main Line to close for nine days over February 2027 half-term for major rail upgrade work.
stories.summary: Passengers on one of Britain's busiest rail corridors face a nine-day shutdown next winter. Operator Greater Thameslink Railway says all lines south of Three Bridges will close from 13 to 21 February 2027, with replacement buses running in place of trains. The work includes track renewal, earthworks and level-crossing renewal, which Network Rail says will avoid repeated weekend disruption during the busy summer season. Some London Victoria to Brighton trains will still run but diverted via Horsham and Littlehampton, meaning longer journeys. Replacement bus details and revised timetables are due in journey planners later in November. Separately, GTR warned of engineering work around Redhill over Christmas and New Year.

stories.headline: 50 feared dead in Congo gold mine collapse
stories.claim: At least 50 people feared dead after a gold mine collapsed in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.
stories.summary: At least 50 people are feared dead after a gold mine caved in near Kamituga in South Kivu province, eastern DR Congo, on Friday afternoon. Heavy rain flooded three tunnels, trapping miners, and local officials said most of the dead were young. The mayor declared two days of mourning, though he said the exact toll was not yet known. Rescuers, some using shovels or bare hands, are digging through rubble. The mine was an informal, makeshift operation and was not on the concession owned by Canadian miner Banro, the company said. Mining accidents are frequent in the country, which supplies more than half the world's cobalt, a key battery metal.

stories.headline: Fed's Collins says gradual rate hikes best to manage economic risks
stories.claim: Boston Fed President Susan Collins backs a steady, gradual pace of rate rises and says policy may need to be higher than expected.
stories.summary: Federal Reserve Bank of Boston President Susan Collins said on Saturday that a steady, gradual path of modest interest rate increases is the right approach for now. Speaking at a Boston housing conference, she argued this better manages the economy's uncertainties and argued against a faster pace to tame inflation that has run above the Fed's 2% target for more than five years. She also said recent price data and a stronger labour market mean the path of policy rates over the next year may be higher than she expected a few months ago. The Fed last raised rates in September, and the 3.75% to 4% target range is widely expected to rise by a quarter point at the 8-9 December meeting, with another increase in January. Comments from Governor Christopher Waller and last week's price data have led some officials to consider a bigger move.

stories.headline: Beware the New AI-Fueled Ransomware Boom
stories.claim: Ransomware attacks on leak sites have spiked, with new AI-assisted groups multiplying and more attacks coming from outside the US.
stories.summary: Ransomware is surging again, with researchers counting nearly 3,000 alleged attacks on leak sites over the summer, a rise of 20 to 40 percent since spring by some estimates. Much of the growth is coming from international victims, and Japan has seen a sharp spike in successful scams as AI lets foreign attackers write convincing Japanese. Around 111 ransomware groups claimed attacks between July and September, with many new operators appearing quickly. One new group, Storm, listed 71 victims in 20 days, and researchers say one lone-wolf operator, a teenager, made more than $800,000 in under two weeks. Experts say AI is helping criminals write phishing emails and handle negotiations, though successful groups remain largely human-run. Analysts warn the sudden flood of small operators may fade quickly, but the threat to businesses is rising.

stories.headline: James Webb telescope finds ice older than the star it orbits
stories.claim: James Webb telescope finds glassy water ice and carbon dioxide ice mixed together in the disk around the young star Beta Pictoris.
stories.summary: The James Webb Space Telescope has detected water ice and carbon dioxide ice in the debris disk around Beta Pictoris, a young star about 64 light-years away. The ice is glassy rather than crystalline, and the carbon dioxide is thoroughly mixed into it at roughly 11 percent of the ice, similar to comets in our Solar System. Earlier searches had failed to find ice there, so the finding resolves a long-standing puzzle. The ice appears to have formed in interstellar space before the planets did, and the team argues frequent planetesimal collisions keep replenishing it. The study, led by Sarah Betti of the Space Telescope Science Institute, was published in Science. It suggests the ingredients for water-rich worlds may be common around young stars.
key_points: Webb's NIRSpec detected water and carbon dioxide ice in the disk of Beta Pictoris, about 64 light-years away.
The water ice is almost entirely amorphous, with less than 7 percent crystalline.
Carbon dioxide makes up about 11 percent of the ice and is mixed within the water ice.
The ice likely formed in the interstellar medium before the planets of the system took shape.
Frequent collisions among planetesimals are thought to keep releasing fresh icy dust.
The study was published in Science, with observations made in December 2023.
